concept.name: Hash rate
concept.definition: Hash rate is the estimated total computational power that miners devote to a proof-of-work network, expressed in hashes per second; it is the primary gauge of PoW security expenditure.
concept.intuition: It is the horsepower of the mining fleet: the more hashes per second the network throws at the puzzle, the costlier it is for an attacker to rewrite history.
concept.mechanics: Hash rate is not directly observable on-chain — it is inferred from realized block intervals against current difficulty (Glassnode: average estimated hashes/second produced by miners). Difficulty retargets keep block time constant as hash rate fluctuates, so price-driven miner entry/exit shows up as hash-rate trends with a lag.
concept.formula: Hash rate ≈ difficulty × 2^32 / average block interval (Bitcoin); units: hashes/s (networks now in EH/s).
concept.failure_modes: The metric is an estimate with error bars, especially over short windows (block-interval luck); falling hash rate after price crashes reflects miner capitulation but can be misread as failing security while absolute security remains high.
concept.misconceptions: Higher hash rate does not speed up transactions — difficulty retargets to keep block time constant; it raises attack cost, not throughput. Hash rate also does not measure decentralization: a few pools can control most of it.
concept.example: Bitcoin's mean hash rate reached roughly 1.1 × 10^21 hashes per second (~1,100 EH/s) in recent Glassnode readings; reversing even a few blocks against that wall of computation is economically out of reach for any realistic attacker.

citations.source: Glassnode Studio - BTC: Mean Hash Rate
